title: Class 12 Maths Book PDF: How to Actually Study From It (Boards + JEE) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 12 Maths Book PDF: Study Guide + Free Quiz
meta_desc: How to use a Class 12 maths book PDF for boards and JEE: chapter priorities, the examples-first method, common traps, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Downloading the Class 12 maths book PDF is the easy part. The students who actually score work through it in a specific order — examples first, exercises next, previous years last. Here is that method, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Every February I meet the same student. The Class 12 maths book PDF is open on a laptop, the NCERT chapter on Integrals scrolled halfway down, and the cursor is parked on Exercise 7.2 — while the eleven solved examples above it have been scrolled straight past. Then comes the sentence I have heard a hundred times: ‘Sir, I have the whole book, but I still panic in the paper.’ Having the PDF is not the problem. Almost every Class 12 student has it. What separates a 95 from a 68 is the order in which you use it.

NCERT is the spine of both the CBSE board paper and a large slice of JEE Main. So this is not about hunting for a better book. It is about squeezing the one you already have — on screen or printed — for everything it is worth.

First, know what the Class 12 maths book actually covers

The NCERT Class 12 Mathematics book runs to thirteen chapters across two parts. They do not carry equal weight in the board exam, and pretending they do is the first mistake. Here is the rough marks split that has held steady for years:

UnitChaptersBoard marks (approx)
CalculusContinuity & Differentiability, Application of Derivatives, Integrals, Application of Integrals, Differential Equations35
Vectors & 3-D GeometryVector Algebra, Three Dimensional Geometry14
AlgebraMatrices, Determinants10
Relations & FunctionsRelations & Functions, Inverse Trigonometric Functions8
ProbabilityProbability8
Linear ProgrammingLinear Programming5

Calculus alone is 35 of 80 marks. If you are short on time, that table is your revision plan. Do not spread yourself evenly — give Integrals and Application of Derivatives the hours they deserve.

The examples-first method (this is the whole trick)

Here is the habit that changes results, and it costs nothing. For every chapter, work the solved examples before you touch the exercise — and work them with a pen, not with your eyes.

NCERT examples are not decoration. They introduce every technique the exercise then tests: the substitution in Example 5 is the substitution you will need in Question 9. Read the example, close the book, and try to reproduce it on paper. If you get stuck, peek, then finish. Only once the examples of a chapter feel routine should you open the exercise. Students who skip this step spend twice as long on the exercise, guessing at methods the book already handed them.

Then the exercises, in order

  • Do exercises in sequence — NCERT deliberately builds difficulty, and the Miscellaneous Exercise at the end of each chapter is the hardest and the most board-like.
  • Mark every question you could not do unaided with a small dot. These dots are your real syllabus for the second revision.
  • Do not check the answer until you have committed to a full solution. Reading a solution feels like learning; it usually is not.

Previous years, last

Once a chapter's exercises are done, pull the last five to seven years of CBSE board questions for that chapter and the relevant JEE Main questions. This is where you find out whether you actually own the topic or only recognise it. Doing past papers too early — before the exercises — just teaches you to feel bad; doing them last turns knowledge into marks.

Board prep versus JEE prep from the same book

The same PDF serves both goals, but you read it differently. For boards, presentation is graded: write every step, state the formula, and practise the exact NCERT phrasing because examiners reward it. For JEE, speed and pattern-spotting matter more — you will skip some of the wordier board-style questions and instead drill the trickier variants and objective-type problems built on the same concepts. A worked NCERT example is your launchpad for both; you just push it further for JEE.

Common pitfalls that quietly cost marks

  • Skipping Application of Integrals and LP because they ‘feel small.’ Together they are near-guaranteed marks with almost no theory — the cheapest points on the paper.
  • Ignoring the derivations in Inverse Trig and Continuity. CBSE asks you to prove, not just apply. If you only memorise results, a two-mark proof will catch you.
  • Treating the PDF as read-only. A book you cannot annotate is a book you will not absorb. Print the chapters you struggle with, or keep a separate rough register keyed to example numbers.
  • Waiting for a ‘perfect’ solution set. You need worked solutions you trust while you practise — not after the exam.

A realistic four-week routine before boards

Two hours a day, six days a week, beats a frantic all-nighter. A pattern that has worked for students I have taught: week one on all of Calculus (examples then exercises), week two on Vectors, 3-D and Algebra, week three on Probability, Relations & Functions, Inverse Trig and LP, and week four purely on previous-year papers under a timer. Keep the dotted questions from earlier close by — that is your personalised revision list, and it is far shorter than the whole book.

Test yourself, then go deeper

Below is a short, free quiz drawn straight from Class 12 topics — derivatives, integrals, matrices, probability and more. Try it, then read the explanations for anything you miss. When you want fully worked, step-by-step solutions to every NCERT exercise to practise alongside the book, the Class 12 Mathematics NCERT Solution Book in the box below gives you exactly that.

quiz.title: Class 12 Maths Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions spanning calculus, algebra, vectors and probability at Class 12 level. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is the derivative of sin(x) with respect to x?
questions.explanation: The derivative of sin(x) is cos(x). This is a standard result you use constantly in Continuity and Differentiability.

questions.q: The value of the integral of 1/x dx (for x > 0) is:
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of 1/x is the natural logarithm ln|x|, plus the constant of integration C.

questions.q: If A is a 3×3 matrix and det(A) = 5, what is det(2A)?
questions.explanation: For an n×n matrix, det(kA) = kⁿ det(A). Here 2³ × 5 = 8 × 5 = 40.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting an even number?
questions.explanation: The even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6 — three of six equally likely faces, so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.q: The dot product of vectors i + 2j + 3k and 2i + j + k is:
What is the principal value of the inverse function sin⁻¹(1)?
questions.explanation: sin(π/2) = 1, and π/2 lies in the principal range [−π/2, π/2], so sin⁻¹(1) = π/2.

questions.q: For the function f(x) = x² − 4x + 3, at which x is there a local minimum?
questions.explanation: f'(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2, and f''(x) = 2 > 0, so x = 2 is a local minimum.

questions.q: The order of the differential equation d²y/dx² + 3(dy/dx)³ + y = 0 is:
questions.explanation: Order is the highest derivative present. The highest here is the second derivative, so the order is 2. (The cube affects degree, not order.)

faq.q: Is the NCERT Class 12 maths book enough for the CBSE board exam?
faq.a: For the board paper, yes — the exam is built almost entirely on NCERT examples and exercises, including the Miscellaneous Exercises. Finish every solved example and exercise question and you have covered the syllabus. Reference books add value only after NCERT is solid.

faq.q: Is the Class 12 maths PDF enough for JEE Main too?
faq.a: NCERT is the foundation for JEE Main, and many questions are direct applications of it, but it is not sufficient on its own. Master NCERT first, then move to objective-type and higher-difficulty problems on the same concepts for the speed and variety JEE demands.

faq.q: In what order should I study the chapters?
faq.a: Start with Calculus — it carries about 35 of 80 board marks. Then Vectors and 3-D Geometry, then Algebra (Matrices and Determinants), and fit in Probability, Relations & Functions, Inverse Trigonometry and Linear Programming around them. Weight your hours by marks, not by chapter order.

faq.q: Should I read the solved examples or go straight to the exercises?
faq.a: Always work the solved examples first, with a pen, before the exercise. Each example introduces the exact technique the exercise then tests. Skipping them is why students find the exercises so much harder than they need to be.
